content: The application of botulinum toxin as a treatment for strabismus has been extensively documented in medical literature. However, its comparative effectiveness against other treatment modalities, such as surgery or conservative therapies, remains uncertain. The primary aim of this review was to evaluate the efficacy of botulinum toxin therapy in treating strabismus compared to alternative treatments, including surgical and non-surgical options. The review also sought to identify specific types of strabismus that might benefit most from botulinum toxin, such as small-angle strabismus or cases with binocular potential (the ability to use both eyes together). Secondary objectives included assessing the dose-response relationship and the complication rates associated with botulinum toxin use. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, and three clinical trial registries, on July 6, 2022. No restrictions were applied regarding language or publication date. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing botulinum toxin with surgical interventions, alternative pharmacological treatments (e.g., bupivacaine), or conservative therapies such as orthoptic exercises, prisms, or lens therapy. Ultimately, the review included four RCTs that compared botulinum toxin with strabismus surgery. The four included studies involved 242 participants, comprising adults with esotropia or exotropia, children with acquired esotropia, and children with infantile esotropia. The follow-up periods ranged from six to 36 months. Two studies were conducted in Spain, while the others were conducted in Canada and South Africa. The studies exhibited varying levels of bias, with none being classified as low risk across all domains. All four studies reported the proportion of participants who achieved improvement or correction of strabismus, defined as alignment within ≤10 prism diopters (PD) at six months (two studies) or ≤8 PD at one year (two studies). The evidence, rated as low certainty, suggested that surgical intervention might be more effective than botulinum toxin in improving or correcting strabismus (risk ratio [RR] 0.72, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.53 to 0.99; I² = 50%; 4 studies, 242 participants). One study involving 110 children with infantile esotropia indicated that surgery might reduce the need for additional surgical interventions, but the evidence was very uncertain (RR 3.05, 95% CI 1.34 to 6.91; 1 study, 101 participants). Two studies conducted in Spain compared botulinum toxin with surgery in children requiring retreatment for acquired or infantile esotropia. These studies provided low-certainty evidence that botulinum toxin may have little to no effect on achieving sensory fusion (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.23; I² = 0%; 2 studies, 102 participants) or stereopsis (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.25; I² = 0%; 2 studies, 102 participants) compared to surgery. Adverse events were reported in three studies. Among participants treated with botulinum toxin, partial transient ptosis occurred in 16.7% to 37.0% of cases, and transient vertical deviation was observed in 5.6% to 18.5% of cases. In one study, 44.7% of participants in the surgery group reported discomfort. No serious adverse events or post-intervention quality-of-life outcomes were reported in any of the studies. The authors concluded that the evidence remains insufficient to determine whether botulinum toxin can serve as an independent alternative to strabismus surgery for certain types of strabismus. Low-certainty evidence suggests that surgery may be more effective than botulinum toxin in improving or correcting strabismus across various types and age groups. Additionally, botulinum toxin appears to have little to no effect on achieving binocular single vision in children with acquired or infantile esotropia. There was insufficient evidence to draw conclusions regarding the need for additional surgeries, quality of life, or serious adverse events. Three ongoing trials were identified that compare botulinum toxin with conventional surgical treatments for different types of strabismus. These trials are expected to provide more robust evidence. Future studies should be rigorously designed, with appropriate data analysis and comprehensive reporting, to ensure high-certainty evidence. Additionally, future research should evaluate quality of life and cost-effectiveness alongside clinical and safety outcomes.
